# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why1: Right after I set the first real step (order a pair with free returns), asking whether to turn that into an email ask at the end is the obvious next thing before the study goes out.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is a startup word I know, but for selling glasses with free returns it reads a little oddly, though the hint makes clear it just means an email line at the end.
screens.why3: Whether I want early wearers' emails is entirely my own call as the founder.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, and the two options are distinct and plain.
screens.why5: My step was "order a pair with free returns", but the respondent's line is a generic "Would you try this for real?", which drifts a little from the order I typed.
screens.instead: Ask people who say yes to leave their email so you can offer them a pair with free returns? (Yes, ask them / No)

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out, after the pilot offer, so it is obvious why it is asked here.
screens.why2: The choice itself is simple, but 'aduts' is a typo (after 'adut' on screen 10) that makes me read the question twice.
screens.why3: Picking a voice and face for my own study is something I can do just by tapping to hear each one.
screens.why4: Daphne and Saskia are distinct and playable, but for deaf and hard-of-hearing people I would expect a text-only or captioned-video choice with no voice to pay for, and it is missing even though the hint says every question is also written on screen.
screens.why5: My actor is still there, but it is misspelled as 'aduts', which drifts from 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' as I typed it and looks careless to a founder whose whole product is getting words right.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? (every question is also captioned on screen) — Daphne ▶ / Saskia ▶ / No voice, written questions only

screens.why1: Choosing how respondents answer belongs right before sending, after I've picked who asks the questions.
screens.why2: The choices read plainly, but the status lines 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' and 'Ready when Daphne is' need a second read to see they mean Daphne's video isn't finished yet.
screens.why3: I know my wearers well enough to know whether they'd rather read and tap or face a talking interviewer, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The three choices are complete and distinct, but the AI option sells itself on hearing her aloud ('Hear her') and on catching speech in loud rooms, which is the wrong pitch for deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents; it never says her video is captioned, and it doesn't flag that speech recognition may miss deaf speakers' voices.
screens.why5: The screen keeps my respondents as deaf and hard-of-hearing adults and leaks nothing of AirCaps to them.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? — AI interviewer Daphne (captioned video; they answer by typing, tapping or speaking) · Read and tap (ready now) · Let them choose (both offered once Daphne's video is ready)

screens.why1: After choosing how people answer, deciding who gets a link is the obvious last step before sending the interviews.
screens.why2: The three choices are plain to me as a founder: people I know, a Keel contact list, or one open link posted to a group.
screens.why3: I know whether I am reaching deaf and hard-of-hearing adults I know personally or posting in a community where they already gather, so I can answer from my own work.
screens.why4: The options are distinct and complete, but the labels run straight into their descriptions without punctuation ('People I know by name I send each one...'), which reads oddly on first pass.
screens.why5: Nothing of AirCaps or the wearer role leaks, and my pick of people I know by name is kept.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? People I know by name (I send each one their own link) / A list I found with Keel (from the Contacts page; Keel makes a link for each) / A group, with one open link (I post it where they already gather, such as a deaf or hard-of-hearing community; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits under the title beside the number that decides it, Existing sacrifice at 1 of 7, and the card repeats it against the bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on the stage page, but each card says what is counted, over 7 people, and where the bar sits (5 of 7), so it reads at a glance.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer and Commitment are my exact words, but my Existing sacrifice was a dollar estimate ($200 to $1,500 a year) and here it is 12 conversations a month, and my price was a yearly range ($599 to $839), recast as $599 then $20 a month.
screens.why_b4: 'Smaller than you think' and 'they value it below your price' tell me the direction but not what to do, whether to lower the price, lean on the free plan, or retarget the segment.
screens.why_b5: Seven people is never called a small sample, and 6 of 7 'would order now' stands as Holding up beside 0 of 7 valuing it at $599 without that tension being named.
screens.instead: Not holding up on 7 people: nobody valued AirCaps at $599 or $20 a month, and only 1 of 7 loses 12 conversations a month, yet 6 of 7 say they'd order with free returns, so test a lower entry price or the free-captions plan before trusting that yes.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside its deciding count, 1 of 7 at or above 12 a month against a bar of 5 of 7, and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: I can see 7 people and the bar of 5 of 7, but the marker 'at 5' sits on a 0 to 15 conversations axis. My 12 and the bar's 5 people share one strip, and the unit 'conversations of the conversations they are in a month' is garbled, so I had to look twice to tell people from conversations.
screens.why_b3: It is my Existing sacrifice dimension, but I set it as roughly $200 to $1,500 a year spent today. Here it is restated as 'about 12 conversations a month' with an awkward 'thread ... and the moment' gloss, and it calls 12 'your low' when I never gave a range in conversations.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the result and sends me to the Price card. It doesn't say what this means for the case, for example that people lose fewer conversations than I thought, so I should pitch the glasses on the few high-stakes ones like the doctor, family dinner or work meeting rather than on volume.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is on the screen, it says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and every answer is listed, so nothing claims more than seven people can carry.
screens.instead: Not holding up, a lean from 7: only 1 of 7 missed 12 or more conversations last month (most missed 2 to 8, bar was 5 of 7), so the loss is fewer conversations than you estimated; ask whether those few are the ones that matter most (doctor, family, work) before leaning on frequency to justify $599.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits right beside "0 of 7 at $599 or more, once" and "0 of 7 at $20 or more a month" against a bar of 5 of 7 on each, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Each chart is a set of price bands with counts over 7 people, my $599 and $20 are marked as a band's low edge, and the strip shows 7 against with the marker at 5, so I can read it at a glance.
screens.why_b3: The card prices my glasses right, but it makes the $20 a month look like part of the price, when my Pro plan is an optional add-on over a free plan with unlimited captions, so it's my price, slightly reshaped.
screens.why_b4: The So line just repeats the count, "most often $250 to under $599 (6 of 7)", and sends me to the Insights tab instead of saying what that means, such as testing a lower hardware price or leading with the free plan.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible and flagged as "a lean, not a call", and nothing claims more than seven people can carry; if anything, "fewer than 2 in 3" undersells a 0 of 7.
screens.instead: Not holding up: 0 of 7 would pay $599 for the glasses, and 6 of 7 put them at $250 to under $599. The $20 Pro plan is optional on top of free captions, so test a price under $599 and let people demo a pair before buying, which four of them asked for.

screens.why_b1: The status word Not reached sits right beside its deciding count, 0 of 7 named your price or more, so I know the check never ran and why.
screens.why_b2: The chart's three bars all read 0 and the strip shows only ghost cells, so I need the count line to see that nobody was asked rather than that nobody answered.
screens.why_b3: Ability to pay at $599 up front then $20 a month from money already spent is the belief Keel derived from my price and cost estimate, in my numbers.
screens.why_b4: The So line says the check waits until 5 of 7 name my price, which is accurate but does not tell me to revisit the $599 and $20 price, the real next step.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the seven, names n on every line and calls the result not reached rather than a failure.
screens.instead: Not reached: none of the 7 would pay $599 and $20 a month (six said $250 to under $599 up front, one under $250), so this waits on the price; rework the price before asking where the money comes from.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 decided alone against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts answers to the agree question, over 7 people, with the marker at 5 and six cells for me, so all three are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The title and the belief line are exactly what I checked: the wearer decides and nobody else has to agree.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count but does not say what it means for me, for example sell straight to the wearer and not through family, or that this win is moot while price and existing sacrifice fail.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the count line says this is a small group and a lean, not a call; the So line's flat 'they decide alone' sits right under that caveat.
screens.instead: Holding up, a lean on 7: sell to the wearer directly, since one spouse had a say. But deciding alone won't help while no one values it at $599, so fix price first.

screens.why_b1: The verdict reads Holding up, and 6 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7 sits right beside it, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Six for, one against and none for no over 7 people, with the marker at 5, is plain on first look, and the strip repeats it cell by cell.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Commitment and its belief line, ordering a pair with free returns now, is word for word the step I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' points at an action but does not say into what (an order, a pre-order, a fitting), and it does not warn that a yes with free returns costs the person nothing.
screens.why_b5: The count line rightly says a small group is a lean and not a call, but the So line then says to book them as if the 6 were settled orders, which is a soft overstatement for 7 people answering a no-risk question.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 said they'd order with free returns, a lean from 7 people on a no-risk ask. Put each of the 6 on a real order page at $599 and see who completes checkout before counting this as demand.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on 'Not holding up' with '0 of 7 at $599 or more, once · then: 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month · bar 5 of 7 on each' right beside it, so I know Price failed and by how much.
screens.why_b3: Price, with $599 up front and $20 a month, is exactly the ladder I typed from my own site.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what this means for AirCaps: no word that five of six put the glasses at $250 to under $599 and four at under $10 a month, and no prompt that three want to try a pair before ordering. The 'Keel is grouping what they said…' loader is still showing, so I'm left to draw the conclusion myself.
screens.why_b5: No claim goes past the answers and the counts (7 against, 6 asked, Amaka never saw it) are visible, but nowhere does it say that seven people is a small sample to reprice a $599 device on, and the stuck 'grouping' line makes the screen look unfinished.
screens.why_b6: The quotes teach me things I didn't type: people want to try before buying (a demo on a noisy walk, borrowing a pair for one matinee) even though I already offer 15-day returns. Value hinges on hard cases (audience questions in a big hall, eleven people talking over each other at lunch), a one-sided-deaf user has a free workaround (the end seat), and the bands show where they'd actually pay.
screens.instead: Price didn't hold (0 of 7 at $599 then $20/month, a small sample): most would pay $250 to under $599 up front and under $10 a month, and three want to try first, so test a lower price or Pro tier and put the free trial and 15-day returns up front.

screens.why1: As the first screen it is obvious why it asks whether I talk with hearing people every week, since that is who the study is about.
screens.why2: Hearing people is how I say it myself, but hearinng is misspelled and made me read it twice.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I talk with hearing people each week, I do it at work and at the shops all the time.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it fully for a weekly yes-or-no question and no escape is needed on a gate.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of people who talk with hearing people every week and nothing of a product leaks.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, but the misspelling may be read oddly by the voice and the closing Yes or no from the template is missing.
screens.instead: Do you talk with hearing people every week? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking if I talk with hearing people every week, showing me the idea is the obvious next step before asking what I think of it.
screens.why2: Glasses, live captions and eye contact are words I use every day; I understood it on first read.
screens.why3: I already juggle reading captions on my phone against looking at the person, so I can judge this from my own conversations.
screens.why4: It is a card to read with no options.
screens.why5: The product is named and described on purpose, in plain words, with no odd terms for people like me.
screens.why6: Short sentences, no slashes or brackets, and it says well in one hearing, though 'an app on them' is a little clumsy aloud.

screens.why1: After asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, asking how often I lose the thread is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: 'Miss' is unclear to me: I rarely miss a whole conversation, but I lose parts of most of them, so I'd have to stop and decide what counts.
screens.why3: I live this every day, but counting a whole month of conversations is a guess; I could tell you about this week far better.
screens.why4: The number box is fine and 'None' is reasonable, but there are three escape chips where one would do, and 'I'd rather not say' overlaps 'I can't recall'.
screens.why5: The founder's situation is a conversation too fast or noisy to follow in the last 7 days, and this drifts to 'missed' conversations over a month.
screens.why6: The question says well, but 'or a low and a high; none is 0' is a clunky clause to hear, and the escapes said aloud don't match the chips on screen.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, how many conversations with hearing people were too fast or too noisy for you to follow? (number box; escape: I can't recall)

screens.why1: Being asked what captioning glasses are worth makes sense after the idea card, but it comes right after counting missed conversations and sits under 'What you do today', which it isn't, so it feels abrupt.
screens.why2: Up front and a month are how I already think about hearing aids and caption apps, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I've priced hearing aids, caption phones and apps myself, so I know what a thing like this would be worth to me.
screens.why4: The bands cover everything and don't overlap, but '$250 to under $599' is a strange edge that looks like a sticker price rather than a range a person would think in.
screens.why5: The $599 edge feels like the company's own price slipped into the list, nudging me toward it.
screens.why6: The two steps are easy to hold, but 'or say you can't say' trips when heard and 'five hundred ninety-nine' is a clumsy number to hear as a boundary.
screens.instead: What would AirCaps be worth to you up front? Under $250 · $250 to under $500 · $500 to under $1,000 · $1,000 to under $2,500 · $2,500 or more · I wouldn't pay for this -- escape spoken as 'Or say I can't say'.

screens.why1: I just put a price on the glasses, so it makes sense to ask what would push that price up for me.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd answer straight off, like 'if the captions kept up in a loud restaurant' or 'if it worked with my hearing aids'.
screens.why3: I know exactly where I lose a conversation, at family dinners, the pharmacy counter and work meetings, so I can say what would make it worth more.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: It names AirCaps, which I already saw on the idea card, and it doesn't slip in any other company talk or terms.
screens.why6: It's one short question, but the band read back as 'two hundred fifty to under five hundred ninety-nine dollars' is a clunky stretch of numbers to hear before the question comes.
screens.instead: You put AirCaps at $250 to under $599. What would make it worth more to you?

screens.why1: After I've put a price on AirCaps, it makes sense to ask whether I'd be buying it alone or with someone else's say-so.
screens.why2: 'Something like this' makes me stop and guess whether they mean my hearing aids, a captioning app or nothing I've bought, so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: I've bought hearing aids, and my audiologist and insurer had a say, but I've never paid for anything like caption glasses, so I'd be stretching to answer.
screens.why4: 'No, someone else decided for me' doesn't answer 'did anyone else have to agree' as a no, the two yeses overlap, and the insurance company or audiologist isn't really 'someone' or 'several people' to me.
screens.why5: It asks who gets a say in paying, and nothing of the company's plan or its own words reaches me.
screens.why6: Four longish options mirroring each other are hard to hold by ear, and 'or say you can't say' is a clumsy tongue-twister to end on.
screens.instead: The last time you paid for a hearing device or captioning, did anyone else, like family or insurance, have to agree? Options: No, it was my call alone; Yes, family had to agree; Yes, insurance or a clinic had to approve; Someone else paid for it. Escape: I can't recall.

screens.why1: After the price and who-agrees questions, asking whether I would actually order a pair is the obvious last step.
screens.why2: Ordering a pair of glasses with free returns is plain to me and I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: I decide myself what I buy for my own hearing, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: There is no plain 'Probably yes' between the full yes and 'Probably not', so a hesitant yes like mine has nowhere to go, and there is no escape chip.
screens.why5: The card names AirCaps as live captions in glasses, nothing more leaks, and the question keeps the founder's free-returns offer.
screens.why6: It says well enough, but 'free returns' is said twice in one breath and the shift from 'you'd' to 'probably not' is a little awkward to hear.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you order a pair with free returns, or not? Yes · Probably yes · Probably not · No
